client: I've been feeling really overwhelmed lately with my thesis deadlines creeping up on me, and I honestly don't know how to keep everything together. On top of the thesis work, I have my part-time job and people expecting me to show up socially, and it feels like I'm being pulled in every direction at once. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because at the end of the day the deadlines are still going to be there no matter what I say in here.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a really heavy load right now — the thesis, work, and social expectations all pressing on you at once, and that's genuinely exhausting. I also notice that while you're describing all of this pressure, there's something almost quiet and resigned in the way you're expressing it, like you might be running low on energy even as you lay it all out. You're right that the deadlines won't disappear, but I'm curious — what would it feel like to have a space where we could work on how *you* relate to all of this, rather than trying to make the deadlines go away?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, I'm not sure what that would even look like, because I've tried journaling and breathing exercises before and they just felt like I was putting a bandage on something that needed surgery. I guess part of me wants to believe there's a way to feel less crushed by all of this, but I also worry that if I spend time "working on how I relate to it," I'm just losing hours I could be using to actually get things done. It's like I can't afford to slow down long enough to figure out why I can't slow down.
therapist: The way you put that — "I can't afford to slow down long enough to figure out why I can't slow down" — really captures something important, and I can hear how much urgency and tension is sitting underneath that thought. What you're describing isn't a bandage situation at all; CBT isn't about calming yourself down so you can ignore the problem, it's actually about questioning whether the belief that *every moment must be productive* is itself part of what's crushing you. I'm wondering — when you imagine what "getting enough done" would actually look like, is there ever a point where you feel like you've truly done enough, or does that finish line keep moving?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Honestly, no, the finish line never really stops moving. Like I'll tell myself "just finish this chapter and you can breathe," but then I finish it and immediately I'm already thinking about the next thing I haven't done yet, and there's no moment where I actually feel okay about where I am. I hear what you're saying about the belief being part of the problem, but I don't know how you just... stop believing something that feels completely true and necessary to survive right now.
therapist: What you're describing — finishing something and feeling nothing but the weight of the next thing — is exhausting in a way that goes bone-deep, and there's something almost tender in how softly you're talking about it, like you've been carrying this for a long time and you're tired. You're not being asked to *stop* believing it overnight — that's not how this works — but I am curious about one small thing: when you finished that chapter, even for a split second before the next worry rushed in, was there anything there at all, even a flicker of something?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I mean... maybe, yeah, there was something for like half a second, almost like relief, but it disappeared so fast I barely registered it before my brain was already listing everything else. It feels almost dangerous to hold onto that feeling, like if I let myself feel good about finishing something, I'll lose my edge and stop pushing as hard. I know that probably sounds strange, but the anxiety almost feels like it's doing a job for me, keeping me moving when I'd otherwise fall apart.
therapist: That doesn't sound strange at all — it actually makes a lot of sense that anxiety has started to feel like a necessary engine, especially when it's been the thing keeping you moving for so long. But I want to gently sit with what you just noticed: that flicker of relief *was* real, and it didn't actually make you stop or fall apart — you're still here, still pushing. What if the anxiety isn't what's keeping you functional, but rather a story you've had to tell yourself to survive a pace that was never really sustainable?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That's... a really uncomfortable thought, actually, because if the anxiety isn't what's keeping me going, then what is? And if the pace was never sustainable, that means I've been doing this to myself, which somehow feels worse than just blaming the deadlines or the circumstances. I don't know if I'm ready to look at it that way, because it kind of makes me feel guilty on top of everything else.
therapist: The guilt you're feeling makes complete sense, but I want to offer a gentle reframe: recognizing that a pace was unsustainable isn't the same as saying you *chose* to harm yourself — it usually means you were doing the best you could with what you believed you needed to survive. And actually, the fact that this feels uncomfortable rather than dismissible tells me something important — that there's a part of you that's genuinely ready to look at this, even if another part isn't sure yet. What would it mean for you if we could separate "I've been coping the only way I knew how" from "this is my fault"?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think it would feel like a relief, but also kind of scary, because the guilt at least gives me something to hold onto, like a reason why things are hard that I can point to. If it's not my fault but also not really sustainable, then it's more like... I've just been stuck in something bigger than me, and I'm not sure if that makes me feel less alone or more helpless. I want to believe that distinction matters, but I'm not sure I fully know how to feel it rather than just understand it intellectually.
therapist: What you just said — that the guilt at least gives you something to hold onto — is one of the most honest and insightful things you could have noticed about yourself, and I can hear that even as you're finding these words, there's something that feels quite raw and unsettled underneath them. That gap you named, between *understanding* something and actually *feeling* it, is exactly where the real work lives, and it's not a sign that you're doing it wrong — it's actually where you are right now, which is a real place to start from. I'm wondering, when you imagine what it might feel like in your body to truly believe "I've been stuck in something bigger than me" rather than "this is my fault," what comes up for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: When I try to imagine that, the first thing I notice is this tightness in my chest kind of loosening slightly, but then almost immediately something else clamps back down, like my body doesn't quite trust it yet. I think part of me is worried that if I stop holding myself responsible, I'll just drift without any direction, like the guilt is also the thing that makes me feel like I have some control over what's happening. It's strange because I came in here thinking the problem was just the thesis and the deadlines, and now I'm realizing it might be something I've been carrying way longer than that.
therapist: That moment you described — the chest loosening and then something clamping back down — your body is actually telling you something really important there, that some part of you *wants* to let this go, even if it doesn't feel safe yet. And what you just recognized, that this is something you've been carrying far longer than any thesis deadline, takes real courage to see, because it means you've been working so much harder than anyone around you probably knows. That realization doesn't have to be overwhelming — it can also mean that what we're working on here has the potential to matter in a way that goes well beyond getting through this semester.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That last part actually got to me a little, the idea that I've been working harder than anyone knows, because I think I've been waiting for someone to just... notice that without me having to explain it. But it also makes me feel this wave of loneliness, like I've been doing all of this in silence and I'm not even sure why, whether it's pride or fear or just not wanting to be a burden to anyone. I guess I didn't expect to feel sad in here today, I thought I'd just be problem-solving.
therapist: What you just let yourself feel in this moment — that longing to be seen without having to earn it — that's not a detour from the work, that *is* the work, and it makes complete sense that sadness showed up alongside it. There's something quietly significant in the way you said that, like you've been holding this very carefully for a long time, and maybe part of what's been exhausting isn't just the deadlines but the weight of carrying all of this alone. I want to ask gently — when you imagine not being a burden to someone, whose voice is that, and how long have you been listening to it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That question kind of stopped me, because I don't think I've ever actually traced it back to a specific voice before, I've just always assumed it was true. But if I'm being honest, I think it probably started with my family, where there was always this unspoken rule that you don't make things harder for other people, you just handle it quietly. I've been listening to it for so long that it doesn't even sound like a voice anymore, it just sounds like reality.
therapist: What you just uncovered is really significant — that "don't be a burden" stopped being a rule someone taught you and became so woven in that it just felt like the truth about how the world works. And I notice you're speaking quite quickly right now, like this realization is moving fast through you, which makes me wonder if there's more feeling underneath it than the words alone are capturing. What's it like to see it clearly, maybe for the first time, as something that was *handed* to you rather than something that's simply true?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: It feels disorienting, honestly, like when you've been looking at something your whole life and suddenly the perspective shifts and you can't unsee it. There's something almost grief-like sitting in my chest right now, because if it was handed to me, then I've been punishing myself all this time for something that wasn't even mine to carry. But I also don't know what I do with that, like understanding it in this room is one thing, but I'm going to walk out of here and still feel like a burden the moment I ask someone for help.
therapist: That grief you're naming is real and it makes complete sense — you've been carrying a weight that was never yours, and there's something that needs to be mourned in that realization before you can fully set it down. You're right that understanding something here doesn't automatically change how it feels out there, and that gap is frustrating, but what you've done today is actually the first step: you've found the root, and now we have something real to work with together. I want to hold onto what you said about asking for help — when we meet again, I'd love to explore what it might look like to experiment, just once, with letting someone in and seeing what actually happens versus what that old voice predicts will happen.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
